summary: Defines the Network Access Identifier, a standard syntax for the user identifier a client submits when asking for network access, typically in the form user@realm. It supports roaming and inter-domain authentication, and is a revision of an earlier specification.

eli5.summary: A user name that also says which organization you belong to, like name@school, so a network knows where to check your password.

questions: what is a network access identifier
how are nais routed in radius
how long can an nai be
subtitle: The user@realm format for identifying who is asking for network access, so requests can be routed to the right home domain.

tldr.problem: Inter-domain authentication, or roaming, needs a standard way for one domain to identify another domain's users so a request can reach the user's home authentication server.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Identifier is a UTF-8 string of the form username@realm, with a formal ABNF grammar. The realm is a domain name used to route the request through AAA systems.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7542 revises RFC 4282, fixing its handling of international character sets, and recommends the NAI format for user identifiers in other protocols.

today: RFC 7542 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4282. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Roaming and the Need for an Identifier
sections.content:
In inter-domain authentication, or roaming, a user has credentials at a "home" domain but presents them at a "visited" domain. The visited domain passes them to the home domain, which typically answers permit or deny, possibly with authorization parameters for the visited domain to enforce. The RFC lists interested parties such as regional ISPs, telecom companies, wireless LAN hotspots and businesses offering VPN access.

To support this, the home authentication server must be identifiable, and that is done with the Network Access Identifier (NAI) that the user submits to the network access server (NAS). The NAI may differ from the user's email address.

The NAI also turned out to be useful beyond AAA systems. The RFC only recommends it for other protocols, and it explicitly allows more than one identifier per user, including anonymous ones where identifiers are publicly visible.

The revision of RFC 4282 was motivated by internationalization problems, raised in the context of eduroam. RFC 4282 limited realms to English letters, digits and hyphen, conflicted with 8-bit clean protocols such as EAP and RADIUS, required language-specific mappings that intermediate nodes could not perform, and the RFC states that no AAA client, proxy or server had implemented its requirements.
sections.eli5: When you visit another school's Wi-Fi, they need to know which school is yours so they can ask it to vouch for you. The NAI is the label that tells them.

sections.title: The NAI Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar is in ABNF. An NAI can be a username alone, a realm alone with a leading @, or username@realm. The username is one or more dot-separated strings of allowed characters, which are letters, digits, a set of punctuation, and any UTF-8 multibyte character. The realm is two or more labels separated by dots, so a single label such as fred@sales is not valid.

The username is based on the local-part of an email address as extended for internationalized email, but it does not allow quoted text or whitespace folding, so an NAI is not necessarily equivalent to an email username. There is no requirement that an NAI be a valid email address.

The RFC lists valid examples such as bob, joe@example.com and @privatecorp.example.net, and invalid ones such as fred@example and fred@example.net@example.net. Strings that are not in Normal Form C (NFC) are not valid NAIs.
sections.eli5: The rules say what letters and signs a name can have and that the school part must look like a web address with at least one dot.

sections.title: Length Limits
sections.content:
Devices handling NAIs MUST support a length of at least 72 octets and SHOULD support 253 octets. Octet limits may mean fewer characters, since UTF-8 characters use several octets.

Transport protocols impose their own caps. The RADIUS User-Name attribute is only recommended to carry 63 octets, and since a RADIUS message holds one User-Name attribute with a maximum attribute length of 253 octets, RADIUS cannot support longer NAIs. Diameter allows content up to 2^24 - 9 octets, but an NAI that later gets translated to RADIUS faces the RADIUS limits.
sections.eli5: Names can be long, but some mail slots are narrow. If your label is too long, some systems along the way will not fit it through.

sections.title: Username Privacy
sections.content:
Only the home domain can interpret the username, so other nodes SHOULD treat it as opaque data. It might be "firstname.lastname", all digits, or a random hex string.

When a separate authentication method protects the username, the NAI MAY be abbreviated by omitting the username, leaving @realm. This is RECOMMENDED over a fixed name such as "anonymous", though "anonymous" is current practice and is still permitted. The common case is a TLS-based EAP method such as TTLS: an anonymous outer identifier routes the request to the home domain, while an inner exchange carries the full identifier and keeps it hidden from the visited network.

A sensitive part of the realm can be dropped too, for example using @example.com instead of @sensitive.example.com. Routing needs the realm, so authentication routing is impossible without it.
sections.eli5: You can put just the school name on the outside of the note and keep your own name inside a sealed envelope, so only your school reads it.

sections.title: International Characters and Normalization
sections.content:
Usernames are Unicode encoded as UTF-8. Realms MUST match the ABNF and the IDNA rules of RFC 5891, which in practice means they MUST be registrable as a fully qualified domain name in DNS. Matching the ABNF is necessary but not sufficient, since some code points are barred from DNS labels in ways that cannot be expressed algorithmically. The Punycode form is not applied to the NAI itself; it matters only when a realm is used for a DNS lookup, and applications SHOULD NOT blindly convert non-ASCII names to A-labels.

Ideally, edge systems such as laptops and phones convert local text to normalized UTF-8 (SHOULD) and AAA systems do not normalize (SHOULD NOT). In reality edge systems often pass an opaque identifier containing localized text, so AAA systems SHOULD attempt to normalize. If an identifier can be normalized, the normal form MUST be used as the NAI; otherwise it MUST NOT be treated as an NAI, yet AAA systems MUST NOT fail authentication just because it is not one.

Where a protocol is not 8-bit clean, it encodes the NAI, for instance HTTP writing fred@example.com as fred@example%2Ecom. That escaped form is not a valid NAI and MUST NOT be presented to the AAA system; comparisons MUST use the unescaped form.
sections.eli5: Names can use letters from any language. The rule is to write them in one standard way before sending, so every stop along the way reads the same thing.

sections.title: Routing Inside AAA Systems
sections.content:
AAA systems use the realm as the key in a logical routing table whose values are one or more next-hop servers. Intermediate nodes MUST use the realm without modification for the lookup. Case-insensitive matching of all-ASCII realms MAY continue, but other case-insensitive comparisons can be wrong. Intermediate nodes SHOULD normalize non-NFC identifiers to NFC before the lookup, but MUST NOT modify the identifiers they forward. Next-hop information may include an IP address, port, RADIUS shared secret, TLS certificate, DNS host name or dynamic DNS discovery.

Routing on part of a realm is allowed if that part is itself a valid realm: fred@sales.example.com may go to example.com, but fred@example.com must not be routed to com.

The home realm MUST be the default. Using a different realm requires explicit knowledge that it exists and supports such use. "Decorated" NAIs with prefixes and suffixes for explicit routing paths are NOT RECOMMENDED in RADIUS environments, because explicit paths are fragile and have to be communicated out of band. The RFC notes they are widely used for Diameter routing in controlled frameworks, where it knows of no issues.
sections.eli5: Mail sorters look only at the school part of the label to decide where to send the note next, and they are not allowed to scribble on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An NAI reveals a user's home affiliation, which can help an attacker probe the username space. This matters most where the username crosses the Internet in clear text, as in RADIUS. Transport protection such as IPsec for RADIUS or TLS for Diameter helps, and omitting the username protects it even from intermediate nodes, though not the realm.

Using one identifier across protocols lets an observer track the user and correlate activity over time. The RFC RECOMMENDS multiple identifiers that change over time, while noting that provisioning them is hard, probably why they are rarely used.

Inner and outer identifiers in TTLS need not be related. Systems that permit anonymous outer identifiers are RECOMMENDED to require that the inner domain equal or be a subdomain of the outer one, and a request with disparate realms SHOULD be rejected as a security violation.
sections.eli5: Your school name on the label tells outsiders where you belong, so the advice is to hide your own name and, if you can, change it now and then.

sections.title: Administration of Realm Names
sections.content:
No new administrative procedure is created. NAI realm names piggyback on DNS: the right to use a realm for roaming comes with the right to use the matching fully qualified domain name. Administrators MUST NOT publicly use a realm without owning the FQDN. Private use of unowned realms within an administrative domain is allowed, though example names such as example.com are RECOMMENDED.

Using an FQDN as the realm does not require DNS to locate the authentication server. Existing RADIUS implementations typically use proxy configuration files, while Diameter supports DNS for locating servers.
sections.eli5: To use a school name on your labels, you must really own that web address. Nobody gets to pretend to be a school they do not belong to.

viz.caption: CORE NAI GRAMMAR (ABNF, EXCERPT FROM RFC 7542)

data.title: NAI grammar
data.code:
nai            =   utf8-username
nai            =/  "@" utf8-realm
nai            =/  utf8-username "@" utf8-realm

utf8-username  =  dot-string
dot-string     = string *("." string)
string         = 1*utf8-atext

utf8-realm     =  1*( label "." ) label

viz.caption: EXAMPLES FROM THE RFC, WITH REASONS READ FROM THE GRAMMAR

cells: Realm needs at least two labels
Underscore is not allowed in a realm
A dot must be followed by more username text
